mainTopic: The minimum amounts of oil, water, blood, other liquids, rope, reed grass and paper that make a person liable for carrying them out on שבת
overview: This amud discusses the minimum amounts that make a person liable for carrying things out on שבת. First the גמרא defines the dispute between רבי שמעון בן אלעזר and רבי נתן about the measure for oil, and settles it with a ברייתא: enough oil to smear a small limb of a day-old baby. Next, אביי gives a rule for substances with more than one use. If one use is common and the other is rare, the רבנן follow the common use. If both uses are common, they follow the stricter one. He shows this with wine, milk, and honey. The גמרא then asks why water is measured by its healing use, and both אביי and רבא explain why healing with water is common. A ברייתא then argues about blood, and another argues about how storing an item (מצניע) changes the amounts. אביי explains that storing case with a student clearing his teacher's room, and the גמרא explains why waste water needs a רביעית. Finally, a new משנה begins, giving the amounts for rope, reed grass (גמי), paper, and a tax receipt.

steps.title: The explanation of the school of רבי ינאי is set aside
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא closes the previous line of thought by stating that, according to this approach, the opinion of the school of רבי ינאי is not accepted.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the opinion of the school of רבי ינאי is not accepted.
steps.whatsHappening: This short line finishes a discussion that began on the previous page. It sets aside the explanation of the school of רבי ינאי so that the גמרא can explain the dispute in a new way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the school of רבי ינאי had explained the measure for oil in a particular way. Here the גמרא says that the ברייתא's dispute does not follow that explanation. This clears the way for the new reading in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not so; this opinion is not accepted

phrases.english: And the opinion of Rabbi Yannai's school is not accepted.
phrases.notes: This continues a sentence from the previous page.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion carried over from the previous page.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Under this approach, the ברייתא does not follow the explanation of the school of רבי ינאי.

steps.title: What the two תנאים actually disagree about
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defines the dispute. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר holds that a small limb of an adult and a large limb of a newborn are the same size. רבי נתן holds that only a small limb of an adult counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here they disagree about this. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר holds that a small limb of an adult and a large limb of a day-old baby are equal to each other. רבי נתן holds that a small limb of an adult counts, but a large limb of a day-old baby does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains exactly where רבי שמעון בן אלעזר and רבי נתן differ about the measure for oil. The question is whether two different body parts count as the same amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both agree that you are liable for carrying enough oil to smear on a small limb of an adult. The question is whether a large limb of a newborn is the same amount. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says it is the same, so it also creates liability. רבי נתן says it is a smaller amount, so carrying that much does not create liability.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what they disagree about
A small limb (for example, a finger or toe)
They are equal to each other

phrases.english: And here, this is what they disagree about:
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds:
A small limb of an adult
and a large limb of a day-old baby
are equal to one another.
And Rabbi Natan holds:
A small limb of an adult, yes (he is liable);

phrases.aramaic: אֵבֶר גָּדוֹל דְּקָטָן בֶּן יוֹמוֹ — לָא.
phrases.english: a large limb of a day-old baby, no (he is exempt).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that רבי ינאי's explanation has been set aside, the גמרא redefines the dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dispute is whether a large limb of a newborn equals a small limb of an adult.

steps.title: What is the final ruling?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how this issue is finally settled.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the conclusion on this matter?
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא asks for the final answer about the measure for oil and prepares to bring a source in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far we only have two opinions that disagree. The גמרא now wants to know which measure is the conclusion.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the conclusion about it?

phrases.english: What conclusion was reached on this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a resolution of the dispute just defined.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which measure for carrying out oil is the accepted one.

steps.title: A ברייתא: the small limb of a day-old baby
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא in which רבי שמעון בן אלעזר explicitly sets the measure for oil as enough to smear a small limb of a day-old baby.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear, as it was taught in a ברייתא: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says that the measure for oil is enough to smear a small limb of a day-old baby.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question by quoting a ברייתא. In it, רבי שמעון בן אלעזר gives a clear, specific measure for oil.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here רבי שמעון בן אלעזר speaks of a small limb of a newborn. That is a very small amount of oil. Because the measure is stated so clearly, it settles the matter: you are liable even for this tiny amount.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (a source is about to be brought)
As it was taught in a ברייתא
To smear or anoint with oil

phrases.english: Come and hear, as it was taught in a baraita:
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
Oil: enough to smear

phrases.aramaic: אֵבֶר קָטָן שֶׁל קָטָן בֶּן יוֹמוֹ.
phrases.english: a small limb of a day-old baby.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A ברייתא in which רבי שמעון בן אלעזר sets the measure as enough oil to smear a small limb of a day-old baby.
steps.whatToRemember: The measure for oil is settled by an explicit ברייתא: enough to smear a small limb of a day-old baby.

steps.title: The משנה's measure for water
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next phrase of the משנה. The measure for water is enough to soften an eye-salve.
steps.simpleTranslation: Water: enough to soften an eye-salve with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic by quoting the next line of the משנה. This sets up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה measures water by a healing use, softening an eye medicine. It does not measure water by drinking. This tiny healing amount is what the coming discussion will question.

keyTerms.meaning: To rub or soften (by mixing with liquid)
An eye-salve, a dry eye medicine that is softened with liquid

phrases.english: Water: enough to rub (soften)
an eye-salve with it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַיִם כְּדֵי לָשׁוּף בָּהֶן אֶת הַקִּילוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the measure for water.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: You are liable for carrying out enough water to soften an eye-salve.

steps.title: אביי's rule: common versus uncommon uses
steps.stepSummary: אביי teaches a rule. If one use is common and the other is uncommon, the רבנן follow the common use, even when it leads to a leniency. If both uses are common, they follow the use that leads to a stringency.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Since we see that, for anything that has a common use and an uncommon use, the רבנן followed the common use, even though this leads to a leniency. When both uses are common, the רבנן followed the use that leads to a stringency.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives a general rule for how the רבנן decided on measures for שבת. Some substances are used for more than one purpose, and the rule tells us which purpose sets the measure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The amount needed for healing is usually smaller than the amount used for eating or drinking. If healing is uncommon, the רבנן ignore it and use the larger, common amount, which is a leniency. If both uses are common, they choose the smaller amount, so a person is liable sooner, which is a stringency.

keyTerms.meaning: Since, after all (introduces a known fact)

phrases.english: Abaye said: Now, since
with anything that has a common and an uncommon use,
the Sages followed the common use, even as a leniency.
When it is common and common (both uses are common),
the Sages followed the common use that leads to a stringency.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: מִכְּדֵי כׇּל מִילְּתָא דִּשְׁכִיחָא וְלָא שְׁכִיחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds a general principle that will be used to question the water measure.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Common use against uncommon use: follow the common use. Common use against common use: follow the stricter one.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rule explains how many of the measures for carrying on שבת were set. It is the tool the גמרא will use to question the measure for water.

steps.title: Wine and milk: drinking is common, so the measure is lenient
steps.stepSummary: Wine and milk are commonly drunk or eaten, but only rarely used for healing. So the רבנן set their measures by drinking or eating, which is the lenient, larger amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: Wine: drinking it is common, and healing with it is not common. So the רבנן followed its drinking, which is common, as a leniency. Milk: consuming it is common, and healing with it is not common. So the רבנן followed its consumption as a leniency.
steps.whatsHappening: These are the first examples that show אביי's rule in action. In each one, the common use beats the uncommon healing use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Healing uses only a little wine or milk, while drinking uses more. Since healing is rare for these liquids, the רבנן set the larger drinking amount as the measure. So you are liable only for carrying more.

phrases.english: Wine: its drinking is common,
its use for healing is not common,

phrases.aramaic: אֲזוּל רַבָּנַן בָּתַר שְׁתִיָּיתוֹ דִּשְׁכִיחָא לְקוּלָּא.
phrases.english: so the Sages followed its drinking, which is common, as a leniency.
Milk: its consumption is common,
its use for healing is not common,
so the Sages followed its consumption as a leniency.

steps.triggerLanguage: יַיִן, שְׁתִיָּיתוֹ שְׁכִיחָא רְפוּאָתוֹ לָא שְׁכִיחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the first half of אביי's rule.
steps.raayaObject: The first half of the rule: common use against uncommon use means following the common use, even as a leniency.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The measures for wine and milk.

steps.title: Honey: both uses are common, so the measure is strict
steps.stepSummary: Honey is commonly eaten and also commonly used for healing. So the רבנן set its measure by the smaller healing amount, which is a stringency.
steps.simpleTranslation: Honey: eating it is common, and healing with it is also common. So the רבנן followed its healing use, as a stringency.
steps.whatsHappening: This example shows the second half of אביי's rule. When both uses are common, the stricter one wins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Honey was regularly used as a remedy, for example on wounds. Since both uses are common, the רבנן chose the smaller healing amount. That way a person is liable even for carrying a little honey.

phrases.english: Honey: its consumption is common,
its use for healing is common,
so the Sages followed its healing use as a stringency.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the second half of אביי's rule.
steps.raayaObject: The second half of the rule: when both uses are common, follow the stricter one.
steps.whatToRemember: Wine and milk show the lenient half of the rule (uncommon healing is ignored). Honey shows the strict half (common healing sets the smaller measure).

steps.title: Why is water measured by healing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה. Drinking water is common and healing with water is uncommon, so why did the רבנן measure water by its healing use, which is a stringency?
steps.simpleTranslation: But water: since drinking it is common and healing with it is not common, what is the reason that the רבנן followed its healing use as a stringency?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses אביי's rule to attack the משנה's measure for water. By the rule, water should be measured by drinking, not by softening an eye-salve.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Water looks just like wine and milk: drinking is common and healing seems rare. So the rule predicts the lenient drinking measure. Yet the משנה gives the tiny healing measure, and that contradicts the rule.

phrases.english: But water: since
its drinking is common
and its use for healing is not common,
what is the reason the Sages followed
its healing use as a stringency?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the rule from steps 6-8 against the משנה quoted in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's measure for water (enough to soften an eye-salve).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By אביי's rule, uncommon healing should be ignored in favor of common drinking, which would give a lenient measure.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mistake this for a question on אביי's rule itself. The rule stands. The question is why water seems to break it.

steps.title: אביי: the משנה was taught in the גליל
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the משנה was taught in the גליל. There people drank wine, so using water for healing was as common as drinking it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: They taught this in the גליל.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge by saying the משנה describes a specific place. In that place, water really was commonly used for healing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the גליל, wine was the usual drink, so water was not mainly a drink there. Its healing use was therefore as common as its drinking. That makes water like honey, where the stricter measure applies.

phrases.english: Abaye said: They taught this in the Galilee.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the משנה to a specific place.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Water's healing use is uncommon everywhere, so the משנה contradicts the rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the גליל, both uses of water are common, so the stricter measure fits the rule.

steps.title: רבא: water is a common eye remedy everywhere
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the משנה applies everywhere. Following שמואל, water is the one liquid that heals the eye without clouding vision, so using it for healing is common everywhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: You can even say it applies in all other places, in line with שמואל. For שמואל said: All liquids heal the eye but cloud the vision, except water, which heals and does not cloud.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different answer. He holds that the משנה is not limited to the גליל, because water is commonly used for the eyes everywhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to שמואל, other liquids blur the eyes, but water does not. So water is the usual choice for eye medicine, and its healing use is common in every place. Both uses are common, and the stricter measure applies, just like honey.

phrases.english: Rava said: You can even say
it applies in other places, in line with Shmuel,
for Shmuel said:
All liquids heal (the eye) and cloud (the vision),
except water, which heals and does not cloud.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא בִּשְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to step 9 that disagrees with אביי's limit to the גליל.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the facts: water's healing use is actually common everywhere.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Water is mainly a drink, and healing with it is rare.
steps.terutzMaskana: Water is the preferred eye remedy, because it does not cloud vision. So both uses are common, and the stricter measure applies everywhere.
steps.whatToRemember: Both אביי and רבא keep the rule and show that water's healing use is common. אביי says this is true in the גליל. רבא says it is true everywhere, based on שמואל.

steps.title: All other liquids need a רביעית
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה: all other liquids are measured by a רביעית.
steps.simpleTranslation: And all other liquids are measured by a רביעית.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last clause of the משנה's list of liquids. This line sets up the ברייתא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wine, milk, honey and water each got their own special amount. Every liquid not listed falls under one default amount, a רביעית. The next ברייתא will discuss whether blood also falls under this default.

keyTerms.meaning: A quarter of a לוג, the standard amount for liquids

phrases.english: And all other liquids — a quarter-log.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the discussion of water to the next clause of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any liquid not specifically listed needs a רביעית to make one liable.

steps.title: Blood and all liquids need a רביעית
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that blood and all kinds of liquids are measured by a רביעית.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: Blood and all types of liquids are measured by a רביעית.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that places blood inside the default rule of a רביעית. This is the first opinion, and others will now disagree about blood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה did not mention blood. This anonymous opinion (תנא קמא) treats blood like any other liquid.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
Blood and all types of liquids — a quarter-log.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the משנה's default rule to include blood.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the תנא קמא, blood needs a רביעית like all other liquids.

steps.title: Blood needs only enough for one eye
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says blood needs only enough to paint one eye, because blood is put on the eye to heal a wart.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: Blood is measured by enough to paint on one eye, because people paint blood on an eye to heal a wart.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר disagrees with the first opinion and sets a much smaller amount for blood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He uses the same logic we saw earlier: when a liquid is commonly used for healing, its amount is set by the small healing amount. Blood is used as a remedy for a growth on the eye, so a tiny amount already counts as useful.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who argues on the first opinion
To paint or apply (as eye paint)
A wart or growth on the eye

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
Blood — enough to apply to one eye,
since people apply it for a wart on the eye.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with step 13 about blood.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Blood needs only enough to paint one eye, because it is used to heal a wart.

steps.title: Which blood heals the wart
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which blood is used for this cure and answers: the blood of a wild chicken.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is it? The blood of a wild chicken.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to clarify a detail: which kind of blood is used for the wart. It answers right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds no new law. It only tells us the real-world remedy behind רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's reasoning.

keyTerms.meaning: A wild chicken (literally, an outside chicken)

phrases.english: And what is it?
The blood of a wild chicken.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies the cure mentioned in step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which blood is used to treat a wart on the eye?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The blood of a wild chicken.

steps.title: Blood used to heal a cataract
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל also says blood needs only enough for one eye, but gives a different reason: it heals a cataract.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: Blood is measured by enough to paint one eye with it, because people paint blood on the eye to heal a cataract.
steps.whatsHappening: A third opinion agrees on the small amount for blood but names a different eye remedy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The amount is the same as רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's. Only the illness differs: a cataract, a problem inside the eye, instead of a wart on the outside.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא giving a third opinion
A cataract (a white film inside the eye)

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:

phrases.aramaic: דָּם כְּדֵי לִכְחוֹל בּוֹ עַיִן אַחַת,
phrases.english: Blood — enough to apply with it to one eye,
since people apply it for a cataract.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Agrees with step 14's amount but gives a different healing use.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Blood needs only enough to paint one eye, because it is used to heal a cataract.

steps.title: Which blood heals the cataract
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which blood heals a cataract and answers: bat's blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is it? The blood of a bat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא again clarifies which blood is meant, this time for the cataract.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This works just like step 15. It names the actual remedy and adds no new law.

phrases.english: And what is it?
The blood of a bat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies the cure mentioned in step 16, parallel to step 15.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which blood is used to treat a cataract?

steps.title: A memory aid for the two cures
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a memory trick: inside for inside, outside for outside.
steps.simpleTranslation: And your sign: inside for inside, outside for outside.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a short memory aid so you don't mix up which blood heals which eye problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bat lives inside, near people, and its blood heals the cataract, which is inside the eye. The wild chicken lives outside, and its blood heals the wart, which is on the outside of the eye.
steps.whatToRemember: The ת"ק says blood needs a רביעית. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל say it needs only enough for one eye. Wild chicken blood heals the outside wart, and bat blood heals the inside cataract.

phrases.english: And your mnemonic:
Inside for inside, outside for outside.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ties together steps 15 and 17 with a memory aid.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bat blood (an indoor animal) is for the inner cataract. Wild chicken blood (an outdoor animal) is for the outer wart.

steps.title: Storing an item makes any amount count
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says the משנה's amounts apply only to someone who simply carries out. If the item was stored away, any amount makes him liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: When were these amounts said? For one who carries out. But for one who stores it away, he is liable for any amount.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא that limits all of the משנה's amounts to ordinary carrying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When someone stores a small amount, he shows that it matters to him. Because of that, even a tiny amount counts as a real carrying (הוצאה), and the usual minimum does not apply.

keyTerms.meaning: In what case were these things said?
One who stores something away, showing it is valuable to him

phrases.english: In what case are these things said? With one who carries out,
but with one who stores — for any amount he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: how storing an item affects the amounts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's amounts are for plain carrying. If the item was stored away, any amount makes one liable.

steps.title: רבי שמעון reverses the rule
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון says the smaller amounts apply only to one who stores. One who just carries is liable only for a רביעית.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says: When were these amounts said? For one who stores. But one who carries out is liable only for a רביעית.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון disagrees and flips the ברייתא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי שמעון, the special small amounts listed in the משנה (like enough wine to mix a cup) count only when someone has stored them. Someone who simply carries a liquid needs the full רביעית.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says:
In what case are these things said? With one who stores,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בְּמוֹצִיא — אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב אֶלָּא בִּרְבִיעִית.
phrases.english: but with one who carries out — he is liable only for a quarter-log.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Argues with step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The small amounts apply to one who stores. One who just carries needs a רביעית.

steps.title: Everyone agrees about waste water
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים agree with רבי שמעון that carrying waste water into the public domain needs a רביעית.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the חכמים agree with רבי שמעון about one who carries waste water into the רשות הרבים, that its amount is a רביעית.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends with one case where both sides agree: waste water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually the חכמים have smaller amounts for plain carrying. For dirty waste water, though, they agree that only a full רביעית counts. The גמרא will soon ask why.

keyTerms.meaning: Waste water, dirty water that gets poured out

phrases.english: And the Sages agree with Rabbi Shimon
regarding one who carries waste water to the public domain
that their measure is a quarter-log.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a case where the two sides of steps 19 and 20 agree.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Everyone agrees that carrying waste water needs a רביעית.

steps.title: Isn't one who stores also carrying?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא re-quotes the ברייתא and asks: how can storing be different from carrying? The one who stores is also carrying it out.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: When were these amounts said? For one who carries out, but for one who stores, any amount. Is the one who stores not also carrying out?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the first part of the ברייתא again so that it can challenge it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No one is liable just for putting something away in a drawer. Liability comes only from carrying it into another domain. So the contrast between 'storing' and 'carrying' in the ברייתא seems to make no sense.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master said (re-quotes a source in order to discuss it)

steps.confusionAlert: Storing alone is never forbidden on שבת. The question is why the ברייתא treats 'one who stores' as a separate case, when he too is liable only if he carries.

phrases.english: The Master said:
In what case are these things said? With one who carries out,
but with one who stores — any amount.
Is the one who stores not one who carries out?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Re-quotes step 19 in order to question it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's contrast between מוציא and מצניע
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Liability always needs carrying, so the one who stores is also a carrier. The two categories seem to collapse into one.

steps.title: A student clearing his teacher's room
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains: a student clears out his teacher's room. If the item is valuable to everyone, he is liable. If not, he is liable only if his teacher had stored it.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Here we are dealing with a student whose teacher told him, 'Go clear the place for me for a meal.' He went and cleared it. For something important to everyone, he is liable for it. For something not important to everyone, if his teacher had stored it, he is liable for it, and if not, he is not liable.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question by explaining that the one who stored the item and the one who carries it are two different people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'storer' is the teacher and the 'carrier' is the student. An item that matters to everyone makes the student liable at the normal amount. A small item that matters to no one makes him liable only if his teacher had stored it, because the teacher's storing gave the item importance, and the student acts on his teacher's behalf.

keyTerms.meaning: With what case are we dealing here?

steps.whatToRemember: An item that someone stored away becomes important, even if it is tiny. Someone who carries it out for that person can be liable for any amount.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
With what are we dealing here?
With a student whose teacher said to him:
Go and clear the place for me for a meal.
He went and cleared it for him.
An item important to all — he is liable for it;
an item that is not important to all,
if his teacher stored it — he is liable for it,
and if not — he is not liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (אוקימתא): the one who stores and the one who carries are different people.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'One who stores' seemed to mean the same person who carries, which made the contrast pointless.
steps.terutzMaskana: The teacher stores and the student carries. The teacher's storing makes even a tiny item count for the student.

steps.title: What is waste water good for
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא re-quotes the line about waste water and asks what use it has, since carrying counts only for something useful.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: The חכמים agree with רבי שמעון about one who carries waste water into the public domain, that its amount is a quarter-log. What is waste water fit for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the last line of the ברייתא and sets up a question about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Carrying on שבת counts only for something of value. Dirty water seems useless, so the גמרא asks what use gives it any amount at all.

keyTerms.meaning: For what are they fit or useful?

phrases.english: The Master said:
The Sages agree with Rabbi Shimon
regarding one who carries waste water to the public domain
that their measure is a quarter-log.
Waste water — what is it fit for?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to step 21's waste water rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What useful purpose does waste water have that would give it a minimum amount?

steps.title: Waste water is used to knead clay
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה answers that waste water is used to knead clay.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: To knead clay with it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה gives the useful purpose of waste water.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dirty water is still good for mixing mud into clay. Kneading clay takes a lot of water, which explains why the amount is a full רביעית.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:
To knead clay with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Waste water is useful for kneading clay.

steps.title: Clay has a much smaller amount
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges this from a ברייתא: clay needs only enough to make the opening of a furnace, which is a small amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught: Clay is measured by enough to make the opening of a furnace!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי ירמיה's answer using another ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a small amount of clay already counts, why should we need a full רביעית of water to make that clay? The water amount looks too large.

keyTerms.meaning: But it was taught (in a ברייתא)
The opening of a furnace, where the bellows go in

phrases.english: But was it not taught:

phrases.aramaic: טִיט כְּדֵי לַעֲשׂוֹת בָּהֶן פִּי כוּר!
phrases.english: Clay — enough to make with it the opening of a furnace!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ירמיה's explanation that the רביעית amount comes from kneading clay
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A small amount of clay counts, so the water needed to make that clay should also be small, not a רביעית.

steps.title: Kneaded clay versus unkneaded clay
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: the small amount is for clay that is already kneaded. Nobody bothers to knead fresh clay just for a furnace opening, so water needs the larger amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This is for clay already kneaded, and this is for clay not yet kneaded, because a person does not bother to knead clay just to make a furnace opening.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the contradiction by separating ready-made clay from clay that still has to be made.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Clay that is already kneaded is useful even in a small amount. A person mixing new clay would only bother for a bigger job, so the water to make it counts only at a רביעית.
steps.whatToRemember: Waste water needs a רביעית because it is used to knead new clay, and people only knead new clay for larger jobs. The small furnace-opening amount is for clay that was already kneaded.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this is where it is kneaded, that is where it is not kneaded —
because a person does not trouble himself
to knead clay to make a furnace opening.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא הָא דְּמִיגַּבַּל הָא דְּלָא מִיגַּבַּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: ready-made clay versus clay still to be kneaded.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The small clay amount should also set a small amount for the water used to make clay.
steps.terutzMaskana: The small amount is for clay already kneaded. Fresh kneading is only worth it for larger jobs, so water needs a רביעית.

steps.title: Rope: enough to make a basket handle
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה opens: one who carries out rope is liable for an amount big enough to make a handle for a basket.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who carries out rope is liable if it is enough to make an ear-shaped handle for a basket.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It gives the minimum amount of rope that makes a person liable for carrying it out on שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The chapter's rule is that you are liable only for carrying an amount that is useful. The smallest common use of rope is making a loop-handle for a basket. So that length is the שיעור.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (the abbreviation מַתְנִי׳ marks the start of a new משנה)
One who carries out (from a private domain to a public domain on שבת)

phrases.english: Mishnah:
phrases.notes: Marks the start of a new משנה.

phrases.english: One who carries out a rope —
[is liable for] enough to make a handle for a basket.
phrases.notes: Like an 'ear' sticking out from the side of the basket.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה. It continues the chapter's list of carrying amounts after the גמרא's discussion of waste water and clay ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Carrying out rope makes one liable when there is enough to make a basket handle.

steps.title: Reed grass: enough to make a hanging loop for a sifter
steps.stepSummary: Reed grass (גמי) has the amount needed to make a hanging loop for a sifter or a sieve.
steps.simpleTranslation: Reed grass: enough to make a loop for hanging a fine sifter or a coarse sieve.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves to its next item, reed grass. The first opinion (the תנא קמא) gives its amount: enough to make a loop for hanging up a sifter or sieve.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reed grass is thinner and weaker than rope, so it has a different typical use. People tied a small loop of it to a sifter so they could hang it on a peg. That small loop sets the שיעור.

keyTerms.meaning: Reed grass, a soft plant fiber used for tying
A loop or hanger used to hang something up

phrases.english: Reed grass —
[is liable for] enough to make a hanging loop
for a sifter and for a sieve.

steps.triggerLanguage: גֶּמִי כְּדֵי לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּלַאי לַנָּפָה וְלַכְּבָרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the משנה's list, after rope.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the תנא קמא, carrying out reed grass makes one liable when there is enough to make a hanging loop for a sifter or sieve.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: enough to measure a child's shoe
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה disagrees about reed grass. He sets its amount as enough to take the shoe measurement of a small child.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: enough to take from it the measurement for a child's shoe.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה gives a different amount for reed grass. He measures it by its use as a measuring string for a child's shoe.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A shoemaker would wrap a reed around a child's foot to get the size. רבי יהודה holds that this use, not the sifter loop, is what sets the שיעור. The two opinions agree on the method, a 'smallest useful amount.' They disagree only on which use counts.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who often disagrees with the anonymous first opinion

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
[enough] to take from it
the measurement of a shoe for a child.
phrases.notes: The reed is wrapped around the foot to find the shoe size.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר כְּדֵי לִיטּוֹל מִמֶּנּוּ מִדַּת מִנְעָל לַקָּטָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A dissenting opinion on the reed grass ruling in the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, carrying out reed grass makes one liable when there is enough to measure a child's shoe.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה is arguing only about reed grass (גמי). He is not arguing about the rope in the earlier ruling or the paper in the next one.

steps.title: Paper: enough to write a tax receipt
steps.stepSummary: Blank paper has the amount needed to write a customs or tax receipt (קשר מוכסין) on it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Paper: enough to write a tax collector's receipt on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves to blank paper. Its amount is the space needed to write a short tax receipt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A tax receipt was a very short note, just a few letters. It was the smallest common thing people wrote. Since even that tiny piece of paper is useful, it sets the שיעור for paper.

keyTerms.meaning: A tax or customs receipt, proving the toll was already paid

phrases.english: Paper —
[is liable for] enough to write a tax receipt on it.

steps.triggerLanguage: נְיָיר כְּדֵי לִכְתּוֹב עָלָיו קֶשֶׁר מוֹכְסִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the משנה's list, after reed grass.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Carrying out blank paper makes one liable when there is enough to write a tax receipt.

steps.title: Carrying out a tax receipt itself makes one liable
steps.stepSummary: The משנה ends with the ruling that carrying out an actual tax receipt also makes one liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: And one who carries out a tax receipt is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a final ruling. Carrying out a tax receipt that is already written also makes one liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous ruling dealt with blank paper. This one deals with a receipt that is already written, which still counts as a useful object worth carrying. The גמרא will soon ask why this needed to be said and explain what case it covers.

keyTerms.meaning: Liable (here, for violating שבת by carrying)

phrases.english: And one who carries out a tax receipt —
is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from blank paper to a receipt that is already written. This closes the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Carrying out a written tax receipt makes one liable.
steps.whatToRemember: In this משנה, each material's שיעור comes from its smallest typical use: rope from a basket handle, reed grass from a sifter loop (or, for רבי יהודה, a child's shoe measurement), and paper from a tax receipt. A written receipt itself also counts.
steps.whyThisMatters: This final ruling sets up the גמרא's next discussion: why the משנה needed to say it, and what kind of receipt it is talking about.
